title: Is Interior Office Glass & Partition Cleaning Included in Standard Cleaning or Billed Extra?
seoTitle: Extra Charge for Interior Glass Partition Cleaning? Contract Audit
metaDescription: Extra charge for interior glass partition cleaning? See when it sits in base scope vs a $15–$35/visit add-on, plus audit steps. Compare quotes in our tool.
excerpt: Interior glass is the janitorial task most often described vaguely in proposals, which is how it ends up billed twice or not done at all. This audit guide shows what base retainers usually include, when glass becomes a separate work order, and the exact wording to put in your scope.
quickAnswer: Most base janitorial retainers include spot-cleaning of entry door glass and push plates, but full both-sides cleaning of conference partitions and interior windows is commonly billed as an add-on of $15–$35 per visit or as a project work order at $55–$95 per hour. The deciding factor is the written scope: if the proposal says only 'spot clean glass,' expect an extra charge for anything beyond fingerprints at handle height.

blocks.text: Why Glass Causes So Many Invoice Disputes

In contract audits, interior glass shows up again and again as the line item where tenant expectations and vendor scope diverge. The tenant reads 'clean glass' in the proposal and assumes every partition, door, and interior window will be streak-free each visit. The vendor priced 'spot clean entry glass at handle height' and treats everything else as billable extra work. Neither side is acting in bad faith; the language was simply vague. The financial impact can be meaningful. A 12,000 sq ft office with 50 partition panels might see $60 to $100 per visit in glass labor that one party thinks is included and the other thinks is not.
The solution is to understand the three common ways vendors handle glass, identify which one your proposal uses, and rewrite the scope so there is no room for interpretation.
The Three Billing Models for Interior Glass

blocks.caption: How janitorial vendors bill interior glass and partition cleaning
rows: Spot-clean entry doors, push plates, glass at handle height
Built into $0.07–$0.20 per sq ft visit rate
Partitions assumed included but not priced
Full both-sides squeegee of listed partitions and doors
Separate add-on line on monthly invoice
Full detail of all glass, high glass, film or residue removal

blocks.text: Base retainers in the national range of $0.07 to $0.20 per sq ft per visit almost always include some glass work, but the depth varies. Expect spot detail of fingerprints and smudges on entry doors and glass near high-touch hardware. Full squeegeeing of every partition is rarely included in proposals at the low end of the range, because those rates assume roughly 3,500 sq ft per labor hour and leave no room for 15 to 20 minutes of glass work per conference room.

blocks.title: Red flag phrasing
blocks.text: Proposals that say 'glass as needed,' 'clean glass surfaces,' or 'detail glass periodically' without naming specific panels and frequencies are the most common source of extra-charge disputes. Ask for a panel-specific list before signing.

Run this checklist against your current contract and any competing bids. It takes about 30 minutes with a floor plan and the proposal in hand, and it frequently uncovers either double billing or work you are paying for that is not being performed.

items: Find every mention of glass, windows, partitions, doors, sidelights, and mirrors in the scope of work and task frequency chart.
Confirm whether each mention specifies spot clean, full clean, one side, or both sides.
Check if glass appears both in the base task list and as a separate add-on line, which indicates possible double billing.
Verify that add-on frequency on invoices matches the scope: weekly should be about 4.333 charges per month, biweekly about 2.17.
Look for a work-order approval clause requiring a signed PO before any project glass work is billed.
Identify exclusions: exterior glass, glass above 10 feet, adhesive removal, post-construction residue, and decorative film.
Confirm glass chemicals are listed in the site SDS binder for OSHA HazCom compliance.

blocks.text: When Vendors Fold Glass Into the Base Retainer

Vendors are most willing to include full partition cleaning in the base rate under three conditions. First, when the glass inventory is modest relative to floor area, roughly under one panel per 400 sq ft, so the labor is a small share of the visit. Second, when service frequency is high enough, such as five nights per week, that the vendor can rotate glass across nights without adding labor hours. Third, when the account is large enough, typically over 20,000 sq ft, that a dedicated day porter or zone technician can absorb glass as part of their route. If your office meets any of these conditions and the vendor still quotes glass as an add-on, there is room to negotiate it into the base.

Day porter programs are a particularly good fit for glass. A porter working a lobby and conference zone can touch up glass between meetings using a discreet cart such as the Rubbermaid Commercial Executive Quick Cart, a charcoal caddy cart with quiet casters and a 60 lb capacity designed for daytime visibility in Class A space. When glass is part of the porter's daily route, a separate nightly glass add-on is usually redundant.
When Glass Becomes a Separate Work Order

Some glass work legitimately falls outside any base retainer. Post-construction cleanup after a tenant improvement leaves drywall dust, paint overspray, and sticker residue that can take three to four times longer than routine cleaning. Glass above about 10 feet requires extension poles or ladders and triggers fall protection considerations. Removal of tape, signage adhesive, or window film needs razor scrapers and solvent, which carry glass-scratch liability. These are reasonable work-order items, typically priced at specialty hourly rates of $55–$95 with a $90–$135 minimum. The key is that they should never appear on an invoice without a signed approval.

items.name: Request a written estimate
items.text: Ask the vendor for a scope, hours, and not-to-exceed price for any glass work outside the recurring schedule.

items.name: Issue a purchase order
items.text: Approve the work with a PO number the vendor must reference on the invoice, so unapproved charges are easy to reject.

items.name: Schedule with periodic work
items.text: Combine project glass with already-booked floor care or high dusting to avoid a second minimum charge.

items.name: Inspect before sign-off
items.text: Walk the glass with the vendor supervisor the next business day and document any re-clean items.

items.name: Update the scope
items.text: If the project reveals a recurring need, write it into the base scope with a defined frequency rather than issuing repeat work orders.

blocks.text: Model Scope Language You Can Copy

Clear language eliminates most disputes. A workable recurring clause reads: 'Vendor shall spot clean all entry and conference room door glass, sidelights, and push plates at each service visit. Vendor shall clean both sides of all interior glass partitions listed in Exhibit B, using squeegee and microfiber, on a weekly basis. Glass above 10 feet, exterior glass, adhesive or film removal, and post-construction cleaning are excluded and will be performed only upon written work-order approval.' Attach a floor plan as Exhibit B marking each panel. This mirrors how the vendor's estimator thinks about labor, so pricing will be more accurate and the invoice will match.

Even consumables and minor supplies can blur scope. Some vendors bundle conference room restocking, such as Kleenex Professional Facial Tissue Cube Boxes, a 2-ply, FSC-certified cube format, along with glass detail in a conference room package, while trash liners like Genuine Joe 1.5-mil 33x39 heavy-duty liners may be supplied by the vendor or the tenant. If you see a conference room package line, confirm whether glass is part of it before paying a separate glass add-on as well.

blocks.title: Insurance and safety check
blocks.text: Before approving any project glass work, confirm the vendor's certificate of insurance is current, names your company and landlord as additional insureds, and that technicians using ladders for high glass are trained under OSHA walking-working surfaces rules.

faqs.q: Is interior glass cleaning normally included in a standard office cleaning contract?
faqs.a: Spot cleaning of entry door glass and handle-height fingerprints is normally included in standard contracts. Full both-sides cleaning of conference partitions and interior windows is often an add-on of $15–$35 per visit for small and mid-size offices, unless the scope specifically names those panels and a frequency. Always check the task frequency chart rather than relying on general phrases.

faqs.q: How can I tell if I am being double billed for glass?
faqs.a: Look for glass tasks in the base scope task list and also as a separate add-on line on the invoice. If both describe the same panels at the same frequency, you may be paying twice. Also count add-on charges per month; weekly glass should show about 4.333 charges per month on average, not five every month.

faqs.q: What glass work should always require a separate work order?
faqs.a: Post-construction glass cleaning, adhesive or film removal, glass above roughly 10 feet, and any cleanup involving bodily fluids should require a written work order. These tasks involve higher labor, special tools, or OSHA-regulated procedures such as bloodborne pathogen protocols and ladder safety, so they are priced separately at specialty hourly rates.

faqs.q: Can I negotiate glass into the base rate?
faqs.a: Often yes, especially if you have five-night service, a day porter, or more than 20,000 sq ft. Vendors can rotate glass across nights or assign it to a porter route without adding labor hours. Ask for a revised quote with glass included and compare the total monthly cost against the base-plus-add-on structure.

faqs.q: What documentation should I request for glass chemicals?
faqs.a: Request Safety Data Sheets for every glass and disinfectant product the vendor uses on site, and confirm secondary spray bottles are labeled under OSHA Hazard Communication rules. If your office follows a green cleaning policy, confirm products meet Green Seal GS-37 or EPA Safer Choice standards.
